name: Bissa, Barka dialect

catalog_quote: When asked, most Bissa speakers will say that Bissa has three tones, and cite the following minimal triplet as proof: [gɛ́r] ‘someone’ [gɛ̄r] ‘road’ [gɛ̀r] ‘stone’ In the existing documents discussing Bissa however, there is a wide range of opinion regarding the tone system. In his grammar of the Lebri dialect, Anthony Naden doesn’t address the question of tone. Where he does come close to discussing tone, he refers to it as intonation and simply states that “There is very little use of suprasegmental phonological features in the Syntax of Bisa.” (Naden 1973: 244) This lack of treatment of tone has led some people to conclude that Bissa is a toneless language – see for instance the posting for Bissa on WALS. Schreiber suggests that Bissa may be a pitch-accent language, rather than a tonal language (Schreiber 2000: 60). ... We therefore conclude, as did Galbane, that Bissa Barka has two …

(Naden 1973: 244) [...] Schreiber suggests that Bissa may be a pitch-accent language, rather than a tonal language (Schreiber 2000: 60). new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (18 pp., extracted text, header "Mandenkan, No. 56, pp. 77-94", author Pamela Morris, SIL Burkina Faso). All three pieces of the composite quote are there verbatim: p. 78 "In his grammar of the Lebri dialect, Anthony Naden doesn't address the question of tone. Where he does come close to discussing tone, he refers to it as intonation and simply states that "There is very little use of suprasegmental phonological features in the Syntax of Bisa." (Naden 1973: 244)"; p. 78 "Schreiber suggests that Bissa may be a pitch accent language, rather than a tonal language (Schreiber 2000: 60)."; p. 81 "We therefore conclude, as did Galbane, that Bissa Barka has two level tones, H and L and four…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Bissa is a tone language: two level tones H and L, distributed over the word as one of four word melodies (H, HL, L, LH) regardless of syllable count; a mid tone perceived by speakers is the surface realisation of the LH melody in isolation. No source opened says where word stress falls; the only remarks on non-tonal prominence are second-hand (Naden 1973 saw little use of suprasegmentals; Schreiber 2000 floated a pitch accent analysis, which Morris does not adopt).
new_statements.secondary_stress: not mentioned in any opened source
new_statements.exceptions: Tonal processes only: LH realised as L in isolation, final L falls, L-tone spread, restriction on L+L; earlier authors disagree on 2 vs 3 tones (Prost 1950, Zouré 1975, Bambara 1980, Monet 1989 three tones; Hidden 1982, Galbane 1985, Vanhoudt 1992, Morris 2016 two tones plus downstep/melodies). WALS 13A codes Bisa 'No tones' from Naden 1973, which Morris rejects.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone melodies on simple nouns and verbs elicited in isolation and in short phrases (250 items, Garango speakers), then pronouns in clauses and possessive phrases; Barka dialect. Vanhoudt's Lebir (Zabré) data use H, B and H-abaissé tones.
new_statements.identity_note: Morris 2016 describes the Barka dialect as spoken in Garango (Glottolog bark1245 'Barka (Burkina Faso)'); the Vanhoudt items describe the Lebir dialect of Zabré (lebi1240 Lebir / lere1242 Lere). The two dialects are reported as mutually unintelligible (Vanhoudt 1992: 83) but both are analysed as two-tone systems by their best sources. Glottolog's listing of Wood 2014 'Categorial Grammars' under biss1248 is a misattribution (not about Bissa).

sources.locator: Sect. 2 'Levels of tone', p. 78 (literature review) and p. 81 (conclusion of sect. 2); restated in sect. 5 Conclusion, p. 91
sources.note: Sect. 2 'Levels of tone' (pp. 77-81) and Conclusion (p. 91): Bissa Barka has two level tones H and L combining into four word melodies H, HL, L, LH (established by a 250-word card-sort with speakers of Garango). No statement on word stress; reports second-hand that Naden 1973: 244 found 'very little use of suprasegmental phonological features in the Syntax of Bisa' and that Schreiber 2000: 60 'suggests that Bissa may be a pitch accent language, rather than a tonal language'; rejects the WALS 'no tones' coding.
